'''Edward Norton Lorenz''' (May 23, 1917{{snd}} April 16, 2008) was an American mathematician and [[meteorologist]] who established the theoretical basis of weather and [[predictability#In weather and climate|climate predictability]], as well as the basis for computer-aided [[atmospheric physics]] and [[meteorology]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Palmer |first=T. N. |year=2009 |title=Edward Norton Lorenz. 23 May 1917 -- 16 April 2008 |journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] |volume=55 |pages=139–155 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2009.0004 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Physics today">{{Cite journal |last=Tim Palmer |year=2008 |title=Edward Norton Lorenz |journal=[[Physics Today]] |volume=61 |issue=9 |pages=81–82 |bibcode=2008PhT....61i..81P |doi=10.1063/1.2982132|doi-access=free }}</ref> He founded modern [[chaos theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]] focusing on the behavior of [[dynamical system]]s that are highly sensitive to [[initial conditions]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Motter A. E. |author2=Campbell D. K. |year=2013 |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/chaos-at-fifty |title=Chaos at fifty |journal=[[Physics Today]] |volume=66 |issue=5 |pages=27–33 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.1977}}</ref>

His discovery of [[deterministic chaos]] "profoundly influenced a wide range of basic sciences and brought about one of the most dramatic changes in mankind's view of nature since Sir Isaac Newton", according to the committee that awarded him the 1991 [[Kyoto Prize]] for basic sciences in the field of earth and planetary sciences.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kenneth Chang |date=2008-04-17 |title=Edward N. Lorenz, a Meteorologist and a Father of Chaos Theory, Dies at 90 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/17/us/17lorenz.html?ref=us |access-date=2019-04-01}}</ref>

==Early life==
Lorenz was born in 1917 in [[West Hartford, Connecticut]].<ref name="mit_tt">{{Cite web |year=1991 |title=Lorenz Receives 1991 Kyoto Prize |url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/tt/1991/24996/24998.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080923013324/http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/tt/1991/24996/24998.html |archive-date=September 23, 2008 |publisher=MIT News Office}}</ref> He acquired an early love of science from both sides of his family. His father, Edward Henry Lorenz (1882–1956), majored in mechanical engineering at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], and his maternal grandfather, [[Lewis M.&nbsp;Norton]], developed the first course in chemical engineering at [[MIT]] in 1888. Meanwhile, his mother, Grace Peloubet Norton (1887–1943), instilled in Lorenz a deep interest in games, particularly chess.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Emanuel |first=Kerry |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/lorenz-edward.pdf |title=Edward Norton Lorenz (1917-2008) |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |year=2011 |location=Washington, D.C. |page=4}}</ref>

==Education==
Lorenz received a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Dartmouth College]] in 1938 and a master's degree in mathematics from [[Harvard]] in 1940. He worked as a [[weather forecasting|weather forecaster]] for the [[United States Army Air Forces]] during [[World War&nbsp;II]], leading him to pursue graduate studies in meteorology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="Kenneth Chang" /> He earned both a master's and doctoral degree in [[meteorology]] from [[MIT]] in 1943 and 1948.

His doctoral dissertation, titled "A Method of Applying the Hydrodynamic and Thermodynamic Equations to Atmospheric Models" and written under advisor [[James Murdoch Austin]], described an application of fluid dynamical equations to the practical problem of predicting the motion of storms.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Lorenz |first=E. N. |title=A method of applying the hydrodynamic and thermodynamic equations to atmospheric model |degree=Thesis Sc.D. |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Dept. of Meteorology |year=1948 |hdl=1721.1/44688}}</ref>

==Scientific career==
Lorenz spent the entirety of his scientific career at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. In 1948, he joined the MIT Department of Meteorology as a research scientist. In 1955, he became an assistant professor in the department and was promoted to professor in 1962. From 1977 to 1981, Lorenz served as head of the Department of Meteorology at MIT. In 1983, the MIT Department of Meteorology and Physical Oceanography merged with the Department of Geology to become the current MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, where Lorenz remained a professor before becoming an emeritus professor in 1987.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2008-04-30 |title=Edward Lorenz, father of chaos theory and butterfly effect, dies at 90 |work=[[MIT Tech Talk]] |url=https://news.mit.edu//2008/techtalk52-24.pdf |access-date=2019-04-01}}</ref>

===Atmospheric circulation===
In the late 1940s and early 1950s, Lorenz worked with [[Victor Starr]] on the General Circulation Project at MIT to understand the role the weather system played in determining the energetics of the general circulation of the atmosphere. From this work, in 1967, Lorenz published a landmark paper, titled "The Nature and Theory of the General Circulation of the Atmosphere", on [[atmospheric circulation]] from an energetic perspective, which advanced the concept of [[available potential energy]].<ref>{{Cite journal |year=1967 |title=The Nature and Theory of the General Circulation of the Atmosphere |url=http://users.uoa.gr/~pjioannou/historical/Lorenz-1967.pdf |journal=World Meteorological Organization}}</ref>

===Numerical weather prediction===
In the 1950s, Lorenz became interested in and started work on [[numerical weather prediction]], which relied on computers to forecast weather by processing observational data on such things as temperature, pressure, and wind.  This interest was sparked, in part, after a visit to the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey, where he met [[Jule Charney]], then head of the IAS's Meteorological Research Group and a leading dynamical meteorologist at the time.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Emanuel |first=Kerry |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/lorenz-edward.pdf |title=Edward Norton Lorenz (1917-2008) |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |year=2011 |location=Washington, D.C. |page=4}}</ref> (Charney would later join Lorenz at [[MIT]] in 1957 as a professor of meteorology.)<ref name="MIT News article">{{Cite web |last=Lauren Hinkel |date=31 October 2018 |title=MIT Celebrates the Science of Jule Charney and Ed Lorenz |url=http://lorenz.scripts.mit.edu/wp/2018/10/31/mit-celebrates-the-science-of-jule-charney-and-ed-lorenz/ |website=The Lorenz Center |location=Cambridge, MA |access-date=3 April 2019 |archive-date=3 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403011423/http://lorenz.scripts.mit.edu/wp/2018/10/31/mit-celebrates-the-science-of-jule-charney-and-ed-lorenz/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1953, Lorenz took over leadership of a project at MIT that ran complex simulations of weather models that he used to evaluate statistical forecasting techniques.<ref name=":0" /> By the late 1950s, Lorenz was skeptical of the appropriateness of the [[Linear system|linear]] statistical models in meteorology, as most [[atmospheric phenomena]] involved in weather forecasting are [[non-linear]].<ref name="Physics today" /> It was during this time that his discovery of [[deterministic chaos]] came about.<ref name="Lorenz1961">{{Cite journal |last=Lorenz, Edward N. |year=1963 |title=Deterministic non-periodic flow |journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=130–141 |bibcode=1963JAtS...20..130L |doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1963)020<0130:DNF>2.0.CO;2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Chaos theory===
In 1961, Lorenz, with the assistance of [[Margaret Hamilton (software engineer)|Margaret Hamilton]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sokol |first=Joshua |date=2019-05-20 |title=The Hidden Heroines of Chaos |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-hidden-heroines-of-chaos-20190520/ |access-date=2025-07-31 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> was using a simple digital computer, a Royal McBee [[LGP-30]], to simulate weather patterns by modeling 12 variables, representing things like temperature and wind speed. He wanted to see a sequence of data again, and to save time, he started the simulation in the middle of its course. He did this by entering a printout of the data that corresponded to conditions in the middle of the original simulation. To his surprise, the weather that the machine began to predict was completely different from the previous calculation. The culprit was a rounded decimal number on the computer printout. The computer worked with 6-digit precision, but the printout rounded variables off to a 3-digit number, so a value like 0.506127 printed as 0.506. This difference is tiny, and the consensus at the time would have been that it should have no practical effect. However, Lorenz discovered that small changes in initial conditions produced large changes in long-term results.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gleick |first=James |title=Chaos: Making a New Science |title-link=Chaos: Making a New Science |publisher=Cardinal |year=1987 |isbn=978-0-434-29554-8 |location=London |page=17}}</ref>

Lorenz's discovery, which gave its name to [[Lorenz attractor]]s, showed that even detailed atmospheric modelling cannot, in general, make precise long-term weather predictions. His work on the topic, assisted by [[Ellen Fetter]], culminated in the publication of his 1963 paper "Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow" in ''[[Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences]]'', and with it, the foundation of [[chaos theory]].<ref name="Physics today" /><ref name="Lorenz1961" /> He states in that paper:
{{Blockquote|
Two states differing by imperceptible amounts may eventually evolve into two considerably different states&nbsp;... If, then, there is any error whatever in observing the present state—and in any real system such errors seem inevitable—an acceptable prediction of an instantaneous state in the distant future may well be impossible&nbsp;... In view of the inevitable inaccuracy and incompleteness of weather observations, precise very-long-range forecasting would seem to be nonexistent.
}} 
His description of the [[butterfly effect]], the idea that small changes can have large consequences, followed in 1969.<ref name="Physics today" /><ref name="Butterfly">{{Cite journal |last=Edward N. Lorenz |year=1969 |title=Atmospheric predictability as revealed by naturally occurring analogues |journal=[[Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences]] |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=636–646 |bibcode=1969JAtS...26..636L |doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1969)26<636:APARBN>2.0.CO;2 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Edward N. Lorenz |year=1969 |title=Three approaches to atmospheric predictability |url=http://eapsweb.mit.edu/research/Lorenz/Three_approaches_1969.pdf |journal=Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society |volume=50 |issue=5 |pages=345–349 |bibcode=1969BAMS...50..345. |doi=10.1175/1520-0477-50.5.345 |archive-date=2011-09-30 |access-date=2008-12-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110930080619/http://eapsweb.mit.edu/research/Lorenz/Three_approaches_1969.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lorenz |first=Edward |date=1972-12-29 |title=Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas? |url=https://eapsweb.mit.edu/sites/default/files/Butterfly_1972.pdf |website=MIT |access-date=2022-07-12 |archive-date=2022-01-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220105132833/https://eapsweb.mit.edu/sites/default/files/Butterfly_1972.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lorenz |first=Edward N. |date=1969-01-01 |title=The predictability of a flow which possesses many scales of motion |journal=Tellus |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=289–307 |doi=10.3402/tellusa.v21i3.10086 |bibcode=1969Tell...21..289L |issn=0040-2826|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Quanta Magazine 2019">{{cite web | last=Sokol|first=Joshua|title=The Hidden Heroines of Chaos | website=Quanta Magazine | date=2019-05-20 | url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/hidden-heroines-of-chaos-ellen-fetter-and-margaret-hamilton-20190520/ | access-date=2021-10-23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shen |first1=Bo-Wen |last2=Pielke |first2=Roger A. |last3=Zeng |first3=Xubin |last4=Cui |first4=Jialin |last5=Faghih-Naini |first5=Sara |last6=Paxson |first6=Wei |last7=Atlas |first7=Robert |date=2022-07-04 |title=Three Kinds of Butterfly Effects within Lorenz Models |journal=Encyclopedia |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=1250–1259 |doi=10.3390/encyclopedia2030084 |issn=2673-8392|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In the book "The Essence of Chaos", in the chapter "Our Chaotic Weather" from 1993, authored by Edward Lorenz and [[Krzysztof Edward Haman|Krzysztof Haman]], the authors delved into the challenges of weather forecasting. The work discusses the consequences of chaos in the atmosphere and its impact on weather prediction. They describe a scenario in which meteorologists, in the computer age, generate [[Ensemble forecasting|multiple long-term weather forecasts]] based on different yet similar initial atmospheric conditions. Differences in the forecast results arise due to the sensitivity of the system to initial conditions.<ref name="Lorenz1996">{{Cite journal
 | last1       = Lorenz
 | first1      = Edward N.
 | last2       = Haman
 | first2      = K.
 | title       = The essence of chaos
 | journal     = Pure and Applied Geophysics
 | volume      = 147
 | issue       = 3
 | pages       = 598–599
 | year        = 1996
 | publisher   = Basel, Birkhauser Verlag
}}</ref>

Lorenz's insights on deterministic chaos resonated widely starting in the 1970s and 1980s, when it spurred new fields of study in virtually every branch of science, from biology to geology to physics. In meteorology, it led to the conclusion that it may be fundamentally impossible to predict weather beyond two or three weeks with a reasonable degree of accuracy. However, the recognition of chaos has led to improvements in [[weather forecasting]], as now forecasters recognize that measurements are imperfect and thus run many simulations starting from slightly different conditions, called [[ensemble forecasting]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |title=When the Butterfly Effect Took Flight |url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/422809/when-the-butterfly-effect-took-flight/ |url-status=dead |magazine=[[MIT Technology Review]] |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20170327232113/https://www.technologyreview.com/s/422809/when-the-butterfly-effect-took-flight/ |archive-date=2017-03-27 |access-date=2019-04-03}}</ref>

Of the seminal significance of Lorenz's work, [[Kerry Emanuel]], a prominent meteorologist and climate scientist at MIT, has stated:<ref name="mit-news" />
{{Blockquote|
By showing that certain deterministic systems have formal predictability limits, Ed put the last nail in the coffin of the Cartesian universe and fomented what some have called the third scientific revolution of the 20th century, following on the heels of relativity and quantum physics.
}}

Late in his career, Lorenz began to be recognized with international accolades for the importance of his work on deterministic chaos. In 1983, along with colleague [[Henry Stommel]], he was awarded the [[Crafoord Prize]] from the [[Swedish Academy of Sciences]], considered to be nearly equal to a [[Nobel Prize]].<ref name="mit-news" /> He was also awarded the [[Kyoto Prize]] for basic sciences in the field of earth and planetary sciences in 1991,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Maggie Fox, Eric Walsh |year=2008 |title=Edward Lorenz, father of chaos theory, dead at 90 |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/newsOne/idUSN1632944820080416}}</ref> the [[Buys Ballot Medal|Buys Ballot Award]] in 2004, and the [[Tomassoni awards|Tomassoni Award]] in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tomassoni awards |url=http://www.phys.uniroma1.it/DipWeb/tommasoni/prizes.html |publisher=Dipartimento di Fisica, Università degli Studi di Roma "La Sapienza" |access-date=2013-12-13 |archive-date=2015-09-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924073038/http://www.phys.uniroma1.it/DipWeb/tommasoni/prizes.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2018, a short documentary was made about Lorenz's immense scientific legacy on everything from how we predict weather to our understanding of the universe.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Josh Kastorf |author-link=Josh Kastorf |title=Weather and Chaos: The Work of Edward N.&nbsp;Lorenz |url=https://vimeo.com/287523707}}</ref>

A reprint book containing invited papers on butterfly effects was published to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the metaphorical butterfly effect.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.mdpi.com/books/book/8035 |title=50th Anniversary of the Metaphorical Butterfly Effect since Lorenz (1972): Multistability, Multiscale Predictability, and Sensitivity in Numerical Models |date=2023-10-11 |publisher=MDPI |isbn=978-3-0365-8911-4 |editor-last=Shen |editor-first=Bo-Wen |language=en |doi=10.3390/books978-3-0365-8911-4 |editor-last2=Pielke Sr. |editor-first2=Roger |editor-last3=Zeng |editor-first3=Xubin |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Later in life, Lorenz lived in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] with his wife, Jane Loban (1919–2001), and their three children: Nancy, Cheryl, and Edward.<ref name="Kenneth Chang">{{Cite news |last=Kenneth Chang |date=2008-04-17 |title=Edward N. Lorenz, a Meteorologist and a Father of Chaos Theory, Dies at 90 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/04/17/us/17lorenz.html?ref=us |access-date=2010-05-01}}</ref>

He was an avid outdoorsman, who enjoyed hiking, climbing, and cross-country skiing. He kept up with these pursuits until very late in his life. On April&nbsp;16, 2008, Lorenz died at his home in Cambridge from cancer at the age of 90.<ref name="mit-news">{{Cite news |title=Edward Lorenz, father of chaos theory, dies at age 90 |url=https://news.mit.edu/2008/obit-lorenz-0416 |work=MIT News |date=April 16, 2008}}</ref>

==Legacy==
Lorenz is remembered by colleagues and friends for his quiet demeanor, gentle humility, and love of nature.<ref name=":0" /> He was described as "a genius with a soul of an artist" by his close friend and collaborator [[Jule Charney]].<ref name="MIT News article" />

===The Lorenz Center===
In 2011, The Lorenz Center, a climate think tank devoted to fundamental scientific inquiry, was founded at [[MIT]] in honor of Lorenz and his pioneering work on [[chaos theory]] and [[climate science]].<ref name="The Lorenz Center">{{Cite web |title=The Lorenz Center About Us |work=The Lorenz Center |date=10 June 2016 |url=https://lorenz.scripts.mit.edu/wp/ed-lorenz/}}</ref>

===Centenary celebration===
In February 2018, The Edward Lorenz Center and Henry Houghton Fund hosted a symposium, named MIT on Chaos and Climate, in honor of the 100th anniversary of the birth of Lorenz and [[Jule Charney|Charney]].<ref name="MIT News article" /> The two-day event featured presentations from world-renowned experts on the many scientific contributions that the two pioneers made on the fields of [[numerical weather prediction]], [[physical oceanography]], [[atmospheric dynamics]], and experimental [[fluid dynamics]], as well as the personal legacy they left behind of integrity, optimism, and collaboration. A video produced for the event highlights the indelible mark made by Charney and Lorenz on MIT and the field of meteorology as a whole.<ref name="Celebrating the Science of Jule Charney and Ed Lorenz">{{Cite web |title=Celebrating the Science of Jule Charney and Ed Lorenz | website=[[YouTube]] | date=23 March 2018 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MTwga6dch2s |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211213/MTwga6dch2s |archive-date=2021-12-13 |url-status=live}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Vol.&nbsp;50; 345–349. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720095015/https://eapsweb.mit.edu/sites/default/files/Three_approaches_1969.pdf |date=2020-07-20 }}.
* 1972 [http://eaps4.mit.edu/research/Lorenz/Butterfly_1972.pdf Predictability: Does the Flap of a Butterfly's Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?] ''American Association for the Advancement of Sciences'', 139th meeting. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130612164541/http://eaps4.mit.edu/research/Lorenz/Butterfly_1972.pdf |date=2013-06-12 }}.
